definition: Zephyr means a soft, gentle breeze.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word zephyr. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know zephyr should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: A zephyr crossed the porch at dusk, enough to stir the ferns and nothing more.
A breeze goes past a zephyr — enough to flutter flags, turn pages, and be felt plainly on your face.
A gale claims the most on this scale — wind that bends trees, cancels ferries, and gets ships called back to harbor, as far from a zephyr as the scale runs.

A breath of air is the everyday phrase for the same whisper of wind — one soft stir, felt for a moment and gone. A zephyr is that gentleness with a name and a history: the poet's breeze, soft by definition, kind for as long as it blows.

A waft is a light current known by its cargo — a scent, a seed, a strain of music drifting past on the air. A zephyr is the gentle wind itself, freight or none; if the sentence is about what the air carried, waft is the word.
a violent rush of air that hits all at once
a sharp storm-wind that arrives all at once, often with rain

Zephyros stood at the west point of the Greek wind compass, and his brothers never made the crossing into everyday English: Boreas of the north survives only in the aurora borealis, and Notos and Euros stayed home in the classics. Only the gentle west wind settled in and became a common word.
Zephyr means a soft, gentle breeze.
The chime maker tests her work on the stillest evenings of the year.
Anything will ring in a wind, she says; the craft is in the lightest air.

She hangs each new set on the porch and waits for the faint movement that barely reaches the skin — if the tubes speak in a zephyr, they pass; if it takes a real blow to wake them, back to the bench they go.
Zephyr is the exact word for what she waits for, because it means a soft, gentle breeze — the smallest wind with a name.
Gentleness is not a mood the word sometimes has; it is the definition.
Air that slams a door has outgrown the word entirely.
Zephyr is the poet's breeze — soft by definition, faintly old-fashioned, perfect when you want the air itself to sound kind.
In a weather report or a sailing log, breeze and light air do the plain work.
The word cannot be made fierce: a strong zephyr is a contradiction, which is exactly why writers reach for it when they want gentleness guaranteed.

The rooftop cinema had one enemy, and it was not rain.
Wind above the fourth floor could lift the screen like a sail, so the projectionist checked the forecast obsessively and cancelled at the first mention of gusts.
What she hoped for each night was a zephyr, and most July evenings the city obliged.
The faintest west wind would slide over the parapet around sundown, just enough to cool the audience's necks and make the string lights sway.
It never once threatened the screen; the canvas barely trembled, and the projector's beam stayed as steady as the picture on it.
